Availability of yellow grease increases almost linearly from 50 miles to 100 miles near ORH, and both have volumes sufficient to support a plant. Assuming a yellow grease price of $0.61/kg, the MFSP of the HC via the HEFA-SPK pathway is estimated at approximately $5.2/gge (Table 10) for 50 miles and $4.7/gge for feedstocks from a 100-mile collection radius. The conversion cost without considering feedstock cost would be about $2.8–$2.2/gge. This means that biofuel could be more than twice as expensive as compared to conventional jet fuel with yellow grease. Annual biofuel production is estimated to be 7.1–12.7 MMgge. Yellow grease is not a viable option as a biofuel feedstock due to its high feedstock cost and limited availability within 50–100 miles of ORH. Similar conclusions could be made that it is recommended to pair feedstocks with a larger radius or pair with other waste oil feedstocks, such as animal fats or brown grease, for economic viability. Animal fats could be processed via the HEFA pathway to produce HC including SAF. Feedstock costs $686/ton ($0.76/kg) (Milbrandt and Badgett 2024). Availability of animal fats varies significantly between 50 miles and 100 miles near BAF, but both with very limited amounts. Assuming an animal fat price of $0.76/kg, the MFSP of the HC via the HEFA-SPK pathway is estimated to be more than $19/gge (Table 11) for feedstocks from a 100-mile collection radius, simply due to the low volume of animal fat feedstocks, and cost is penalized by the economy of scale. Annual HC production is estimated to be one-fifth of 1 MMgge. Current HC production is limited to using animal fats alone. Increasing production requires expanding feedstocks and collection areas. Animal fats are currently not economically viable feedstocks near BAF due to high cost and low availability.
